desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

The list is k-sorted: for every pair of positions i < j with j - i > k we have nums[i] ≤ nums[j]. In other words, any two nodes that are out of order are at most k positions apart. Return the list sorted in non-decreasing order.

For example, [2,1,4,3,6,5] with k = 1 is k-sorted and the answer is [1,2,3,4,5,6]. A plain sort costs O(n log n); use the extra information to get O(n log k).
constraints: The list is k-sorted as defined above
hints: Where can the smallest value of the whole list be? Use the k-sorted condition to limit the candidates for the first position of the answer.
The smallest value must be among the first k + 1 nodes. After you output it, the next smallest is among the first k + 1 remaining nodes, and so on.
Keep a min-heap holding a sliding window of k + 1 nodes: pop the smallest and append it to the result, then push the next unread node. When the input runs out, pop the heap until it is empty.
editorial: If a node at index j > k were smaller than the first node, the pair (0, j) would violate the condition, so the overall minimum is among the first k + 1 nodes. Removing it keeps the remaining list k-sorted (distances between the remaining nodes only shrink), so the same argument applies again.

Implement this with a min-heap of at most k + 1 elements. Push the first k + 1 nodes, then for every further node do a push-and-pop of the minimum and append that minimum to the output; at the end drain the heap. Each operation costs O(log k), giving O(n log k) time and O(k) space. With k = 0 the list is already sorted.
